questions.q: How does a server-side Test differ from the UI Test built in Lesson 13?
options: It exercises logic directly — a Script Include method or a GlideRecord operation — with no form or UI interaction at all
It only tests field-level ACLs and visibility rules
It requires an Impersonate User step before it can run
There is no real difference — both step types interact with the form the same way
questions.explain: A server-side Test skips the interface entirely and calls into logic directly, which also makes it faster to run.

questions.q: What does a Script Include validation Test Step actually check?
options: That calling a specific method with a known input returns the value expected for that input
That the Script Include file exists somewhere in the instance
That a form's UI Policy correctly hides a field
That a user holds a specific role before logging in
questions.explain: It asserts the method's return value matches the expected result for a given input — the logic's contract.

questions.q: What does a record-state validation Test Step check, after creating or modifying a GlideRecord?
options: The resulting record's actual state — e.g., whether an insert was correctly aborted or a field ended up with the expected value
Only whether the record's sys_id was generated correctly
Whether the record is visible on a specific form layout
Whether a Client Script fired when the record was created
questions.explain: It confirms server-side logic like a before-insert Business Rule actually produced the correct resulting record state.

questions.q: Why can a Script Include be completely correct while an end-to-end feature still has a real bug?
options: A UI Policy on the form that calls the Script Include could be broken, which a server-side Test alone would not catch
Script Includes are incapable of ever containing bugs
A server-side Test always catches every UI-layer problem automatically
Correct Script Include logic guarantees the entire feature works
questions.explain: A server-side Test confirms the logic layer only; a UI-layer problem like a broken UI Policy needs a UI Test to catch it.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why does real ATF coverage for anything non-trivial use both UI Tests and server-side Tests?
options: Because a bug can live independently in either the UI layer or the logic layer, and each Test type catches what the other structurally cannot
Because ServiceNow requires every Test Suite to contain at least one of each type
Because server-side Tests are deprecated and only kept for legacy compatibility
Because UI Tests are always slower and therefore always unnecessary
questions.explain: A UI Test confirms the experience; a server-side Test confirms the logic — neither one substitutes for the other.
